# What crosses the screen boundary when a Chess cursor moves?

On this handheld, an application does not paint its own window. The application, called a *world*, runs as its own program. A separate *compositor* builds the window and paints it. The world describes what should be on screen and hands that description to the compositor through a `SCREEN` system call. When a Chess player moves the cursor one square, the change on screen is small, but the description that crosses the boundary may be large. This article measures what crosses, how many bytes it takes, and what happens when part of the description work moves from the world into a small view program on the compositor side.

All results in these chapters come from host re-creations. They describe bytes, exact output equality, and host processor time. They do not describe the device kernel, its mailbox, memory peaks, or anything a player would see or feel.

## The two sides of the boundary

Worlds are written in a typed, JavaScript-like language and compiled to RV32 for the device. The Chess world contains application metadata, a key handler, move legality, a search engine, a timer, and a render function, `chessRender`, which converts game state into a screen description.

In the existing design that description is an *ordinary screen*. It is a JSON tree with a heading, a canvas holding an ordered list of drawing operations, an optional footer, and a separate hint string. The compositor parses the tree and gives it to a common painter. The painter uses a shared font and a C rasterizer to fill a 320×320 RGB565 framebuffer of 204,800 bytes.

For host tests we compiled the same game source and the same common reactor to WebAssembly twice:

- G, the generic arm, keeps the ordinary screen unchanged. Its `SCREEN` call carries the existing JSON tree and hint string.
- R, the semantic arm, changes only `chessRender`. It still reads its own in-guest board, and it never reads G's tree. It publishes a compact by-value snapshot of game state, and a receiving view on the compositor side rebuilds the ordinary tree from that snapshot.

Both arms keep the same metadata, key handler, legality, search, and timer code. Both issue real typed-SDK `SCREEN` syscalls. The capture records the UTF-8 tree and the hints as separate fields.

```text
 host re-creation

 world (Wasm build of the typed source)          compositor side
 +-------------------------------+              +------------------------------+
 | key handler, legality,        |   SCREEN     | envelope parse               |
 | search, timer                 | -----------> |                              |
 | chessRender                   |              | R only: closed view (Wasm)   |
 |   G: ordinary JSON tree+hint  |              |   snapshot -> ordinary tree  |
 |   R: semantic snapshot        |              |                              |
 +-------------------------------+              | JSON.parse -> common painter |
                                                |   font + C raster -> RGB565  |
                                                +------------------------------+
```

## What the semantic arm publishes

Squares use a dense index. a8 is 0, the index runs across rank 8 to h8 at 7, and continues rank by rank down to h1 at 63. The value 64 is a sentinel that means "no square", used for the selected square and for both ends of the last move when they are absent.

Each R message is JSON with schema 1 and these fields:

- a 64-hex-digit digest;
- 64 hex digits, one per square, giving the piece on that square;
- 16 hex digits giving eight rank masks. Each rank takes two hex digits, rank 8 comes first, and the a-file is the low bit;
- nine decimal integers: cursor, selected square, last-move from, last-move to, status, promotion hint, completed search depth, node count, and signed score.

The masks mark every legal destination of the selected piece. The world computes them with the game's own move generator, the same code that decides legality. The world also computes the current status, with check taking priority. It does not publish statistics from a search that has not completed. Hidden counters are written as zero, so two states that differ only in hidden values serialize identically and can be deduplicated.

Every message is a complete snapshot. No message depends on a previous one.

At launch, white is to move and the cursor rests on e2 (index 52). The integer record is:

```text
f = [52, 64, 64, 64, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
mask = 0000000000000000
```

The player then selects the white pawn on e2. The selected square becomes 52. The pawn's legal destinations are e3 (index 44, rank 3) and e4 (index 36, rank 4). Bit 4 is the e-file, which is 0x10 within a rank. Rank 4 occupies the fifth byte of the mask and rank 3 the sixth:

```text
f    = [52, 52, 64, 64, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
         rank: 8  7  6  5  4  3  2  1
mask = 0000000010100000
             00 00 00 00 10 10 00 00
```

The piece digits are unchanged, and no field outside the selection and the mask moves. G, by contrast, re-emits the full canvas operation list for the same keypress.

## The receiving view

The R arm needs a program on the compositor side that converts the snapshot into the ordinary tree. That program, the closed view, is handwritten in the typed language (`05-closed-view.typed`). It loops over ranks and files and contains a manual adaptation of the original view's presentation helpers. No compiler extracted it automatically from `chessRender`.

The view receives data only by value. The receiver copies the piece digits, the masks, and an explicit nine-i32 record into one private Wasm page of 65,536 bytes. The view holds no game pointers. It contains no move legality and no search, and it makes no syscalls and has no imports. It writes into bounded UTF-16 tree and hint buffers: 8,192 units for the tree and 120 for hints. The host then parses those buffers as an ordinary tree.

The view preserves all geometry and the original paint order. Operations are not sorted into any canonical order. A per-frame guard caps a tree at 212 operations, and the named fixtures produce between 86 and 148. The view still materializes the full command list on every frame, so the work given to the common painter is the same as in G. The snapshot reduces what crosses the boundary. It does not reduce what is painted.

Admission is narrow. The compositor accepts the view only if it matches a pinned digest and an approved source and toolchain key. It is not a mechanism for loading arbitrary code. Each incoming state is validated before it replaces the last good state. These checks are not evidence that the receiver resists a deliberately hostile program running dynamically, and nothing here should be read as that claim.

## Does the screen come out the same?

The main trace has 127 events across 11 scenarios. The first scenario is an ordinary opening:

1. an illegal selection;
2. a deselect;
3. e2e4;
4. cursor movement while the engine searches;
5. the engine's reply b8c6 after timer wake 78, at depth 3 with 1,600 nodes and an evaluation of 12;
6. a reset;
7. a stale wake, which is ignored.

The other ten scenarios start from initialized fixtures and use the same game logic. They cover:

- promotion cancel, reopen, and underpromotion to a knight;
- both white castlings;
- en passant;
- check;
- checkmate for each side;
- stalemate;
- dead material;
- synthetic signed search statistics.

The trace produces 47 `SCREEN` calls from two independently instantiated real worlds, one per arm. A separately instantiated A/A run, with the unchanged arm on both sides, serves as a confirmation that the comparison itself introduces no differences. One of the 47 calls repeats the previous state, which leaves 46 distinct posts.

For all 47 calls, three outputs were compared exactly against the original, ordered UTF-8 trees and hints:

- the original trees and hints;
- replays into a fresh recipient;
- the full 204,800-byte RGB565 framebuffer, rendered by the real common compositor paint path, font, and C rasterizer.

The A/A, G/R, and M/S comparisons passed 47 of 47 in each arm. M and S, the two ways of delivering the view, are described below.

Four further checks address failure behaviour:

- Lost flush. In a virtual lost-flush test, display state recovered at the next changed status frame, which differed from the stale image in 751 pixels. Recovery after one frame follows directly from complete snapshots.
- Invalid input. Five invalid states were offered, and none displaced the last valid state. A later valid state replaced it normally.
- Generated games. After the design was frozen, a separate extension generated 20 legal-move games using only the control UI, with 200 White moves and the engine's genuine responses. Over 20,109 events, 2,433 complete trees with hints matched. All 220 launch and settled RGB565 pairs were identical, and the games reached 194 distinct piece arrays.
- Limits of coverage. The generated games are deterministic coverage. They are not sealed holdout sessions played by people, and they do not prove the rules of chess correct.

## Bytes at the boundary

At launch, G emits a 4,835-byte tree and a 41-byte hint. R emits 200 bytes of snapshot and no hint. To compare the two at a realistic boundary, the host builds the native JSON `{"tree":...,"hints":"..."}` and wraps it in the outer `{"app":"chess","title":"Chess","frame":...}`, matching the C grammar. The two wrappers add 60 ASCII bytes to each arm. These are host re-creations of two explicit boundaries. They do not run the kernel mailbox.

| Measurement | G (ordinary) bytes | R (semantic) bytes | Ratio | Reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Launch payload (tree + hint) | 4,876 | 200 | 24.4x | 95.9% |
| Launch, both wrappers | 4,936 | 260 | 19.0x | 94.7% |
| 46 distinct posts, full trace | 178,955 | 11,952 | 14.973x | 93.32% |
| 18 changed posts, ordinary opening | 89,651 | 4,683 | 19.144x | 94.8% |

Before measurement, a blind estimate predicted a typical ratio of 20–100x. That estimate was optimistic: the full trace gives 14.973x, and only the opening subset approaches 20x. The same estimate put the view module at 20–80 KB, but the compiled module is 8,641 bytes. A separate gate requiring at least a 5x ratio passed.

The view itself must also cross the boundary once. The approved source is 6,408 bytes and the compiled module is 8,641 bytes. The real eight-byte install header makes the envelopes 6,416 bytes for source delivery (S) and 8,649 bytes for module delivery (M). The first two changed posts of the opening save 9,352 bytes together, more than either envelope. In bytes, therefore, the view pays for itself by the second changed post, whichever form is delivered.

## Host time

Timing ran on Linux x64, Node v24.18.0, on an i7-1165G7. Each cursor or selection class had 1,200 pairs, and G/R and A/A were rotated. Three windows were measured:

- The event window covers the real guest event, the screen conversion, and the copy.
- The receiver window covers the host envelope parse. For R it also covers isolated view rendering, decoding the counted output, and the ordinary `JSON.parse`.
- Timing ends when the parsed input reaches the common painter, before any drawing.

Medians for the selected class, in microseconds, G then R:

- guest and capture: 14.583 / 5.347
- receiver: 28.062 / 37.404
- complete: 46.025 / 44.942

R moves roughly nine microseconds of work out of the guest and adds a similar amount on the receiving side. The median of the paired differences G−R is 1.024 µs. This differs from the 1.083 µs obtained by subtracting the two medians, because the paired figure is a median taken across individual pairs. The unselected class shows a paired saving of 1.166 µs. A fresh rerun gave 1.408 µs for selected and 1.191 µs for unselected, with byte receipts identical to the first run.

The A/A control sets the scale for these numbers. Its selected pair difference has a median of −0.016 µs and a 95th percentile of +6.525 µs. A paired gain of about one microsecond is therefore small next to the per-pair spread of identical arms. The robust result is a change in where the work happens. The total host cost is close to equal.

The delivery method does not change steady-state view speed. Warm median view times were 25.276 µs when the view was already resident, 25.193 µs when the module was delivered as bytes, and 25.410 µs when source was delivered and compiled locally, with 1,200 samples per arm.

## Installing the view

Installation costs more than a frame. The fresh-process figures below exclude process startup and initial filesystem reads, with 12 runs per arm. Median install-to-first-correct-tree times were:

- 1.787 ms with the view already resident;
- 1.936 ms with M, the delivered module;
- 7.031 ms with S, the delivered and locally compiled source.

Within a single warm process, 35 trials against a fresh receiver cache gave a median install time of about 25.9 µs for M and 1,054.4 µs for S. Cache hits took about 14.1 µs and 14.4 µs.

The cache key behaves as specified:

- Adding an initial comment to the approved source caused one miss and then a hit, and the compiled artifact stayed byte-identical.
- Changing the ABI, or changing the artifact, was rejected.

Source installation also affects other work on the same lane. While the host installed from source, the shared worker lane delayed an unrelated `setImmediate` callback by up to 2.026 ms. On the host, this argues for keeping compilation off any lane that serves time-sensitive work. It does not show that a key press on the device would be delayed.

Byte repayment and wall-time repayment have to be judged separately. Bytes are repaid by the second changed post. The host per-frame time gain is about a microsecond, and the A/A spread exceeds it. Source installation costs about a millisecond in a warm process. Any wall-time repayment on the host would take on the order of a thousand frames, and the noise floor makes even that figure uncertain.

## Receipts and the move to firmware

The scripts are in `scripts/`:

- `04-semantic-producer.typed`: the R producer;
- `05-closed-view.typed`: the receiving view;
- `07-replay.mjs`: the replay and equality checks;
- `17-run-host.sh`: the host run.

The results are recorded in `host-summary.json`, `host-timing.json`, `pixel-gate.json`, and `generated-verified.json`.

These host results establish four things:

- the boundary payload for this game can shrink by an order of magnitude while trees, hints, and every framebuffer pixel stay exactly the same across the measured traces;
- the receiving view can be confined to one page with no imports;
- the view's byte cost is recovered within the first moves of a game;
- the host time cost is moved rather than removed.

What the host cannot measure is the device itself. That includes the RV32 build crossing the real kernel mailbox, the compositor's memory under the device allocator, and the time from a physical key to a changed panel. The firmware chapter takes up those questions on the handheld, using the same snapshot format and the same exact-output criterion.
